title: Complex functions and integral transforms
scope: Chapters 1–2 · Complex differentiability, series, residues, Fourier and Laplace transforms

questions.title: Differentiable at a point; analytic on a region
questions.question: Let $f(z)=|z|^2$. Find every point of complex differentiability, every region of analyticity, and all complex derivatives that exist.
questions.hint: Write $u=x^2+y^2,v=0$. Solve the Cauchy–Riemann conditions first, then check the candidate point directly from the derivative definition.
questions.solution: We have $u_x=2x,u_y=2y,v_x=v_y=0$. The Cauchy–Riemann conditions hold only at $(0,0)$. At the origin, the difference quotient is $[f(h)-f(0)]/h=|h|^2/h=\bar h\to0$, so $f\prime(0)=0$. Elsewhere the necessary conditions fail, so no complex derivative exists. Every open neighborhood contains a point other than the origin; consequently the function is nowhere analytic.
questions.rubric: Cauchy–Riemann conditions and candidate point: 4 points; difference-quotient check: 4 points; distinction between differentiability and analyticity: 4 points.

questions.title: One function, two annuli
questions.question: Expand $f(z)=1/[z(z-2)]$ on $0<|z|<2$ and on $|z|>2$. Find the residue at the origin.
questions.hint: Use partial fractions. In the inner annulus use $z/2$; in the outer annulus use $2/z$.
questions.solution:
Partial fractions give $-1/(2z)+1/[2(z-2)]$. In the inner annulus,

$$f(z)=-\frac1{2z}-\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{2^{n+2}},\quad0<|z|<2.$$

In the outer annulus, factor out $z^2$:

$$f(z)=\frac1{z^2}\frac1{1-2/z}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^nz^{-n-2},\quad |z|>2.$$

The residue at the origin must be read from a punctured neighborhood of that point: it is $-1/2$. The absence of a $z^{-1}$ term in the outer expansion does not make this residue zero: the outer annulus also surrounds another pole.
questions.rubric: Partial fractions: 2 points; each expansion with its annulus: 4 points; residue: 2 points.

questions.title: Cauchy’s derivative formula
questions.question: Evaluate $\oint_{|z|=2}e^z/(z-1)^3\,dz$, with counterclockwise orientation.
questions.hint: A cubed denominator calls for a second derivative. Remember $2!$.
questions.solution: The function $e^z$ is analytic on and inside the circle, and $1$ lies inside. Use the higher-order Cauchy formula $\oint f(z)/(z-a)^{n+1}dz=2\pi i f^{(n)}(a)/n!$ with $n=2,a=1$. The integral is $2\pi i e/2=\pi i e$. Alternatively, expand $e^z=e[1+(z-1)+(z-1)^2/2+\cdots]$ and read the residue $e/2$.
questions.rubric: Locate the interior pole: 3 points; correct formula and derivative order: 4 points; result: 5 points.

questions.title: A rational integral on the half-line
questions.question: Use residues to evaluate $I=\int_0^\infty dx/[(x^2+1)(x^2+4)]$.
questions.hint: Extend to the whole real line. The upper-half-plane poles are $i,2i$.
questions.solution:
The integrand is even, so $2I$ equals the whole-line integral. The upper-half-plane residues are

$$R_i=\frac1{2i(4-1)}=\frac1{6i},\qquad R_{2i}=\frac1{4i(1-4)}=-\frac1{12i}.$$

The large semicircle contributes $O(R^{-3})\to0$. Therefore $2I=2\pi i(1/(6i)-1/(12i))=\pi/6$, giving $I=\pi/12$. Partial fractions $\frac13[1/(x^2+1)-1/(x^2+4)]$ provide an independent check.
questions.rubric: Evenness: 3 points; each residue: 3 points; vanishing arc: 2 points; result: 3 points.

questions.title: Fourier transform of a decaying exponential
questions.question: With convention $F(k)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)e^{-ikx}dx$, find the transform of $f(x)=e^{-a|x|}$ ($a>0$). Explain why it is real and even.
questions.hint: Split the integral at $x=0$. Integrate the two exponentials separately.
questions.solution:
The positive half-line gives $1/(a+ik)$. On the negative half-line, substitute $t=-x$ to obtain $1/(a-ik)$. Adding gives

$$F(k)=\frac1{a+ik}+\frac1{a-ik}=\frac{2a}{a^2+k^2}.$$

Since $f$ is real and even, the sine part integrates to zero and the cosine part is real and even. Also $F(0)=2/a$ equals $\int f dx$, which checks the normalization.
questions.rubric: Split the integral: 4 points; calculation: 5 points; symmetry and check: 3 points.

questions.title: Fourier series of a sawtooth
questions.question: Extend $f(x)=x$ on $0<x<2\pi$ periodically with period $2\pi$. Find its real Fourier series and the series values at $x=0,2\pi$.
questions.hint: The constant term is $a_0/2$. Use integration by parts for $b_n$.
questions.solution:
Use convention $f\sim a_0/2+\sum_{n\ge1}(a_n\cos nx+b_n\sin nx)$:

$$a_0=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}x\,dx=2\pi,\quad a_n=0,\quad b_n=\frac1\pi\int_0^{2\pi}x\sin nx\,dx=-\frac2n.$$

Thus $f(x)=\pi-2\sum_{n=1}^\infty\sin(nx)/n$ and $0<x<2\pi$. At each periodic join, the one-sided limits are $2\pi$ and $0$; the series converges to their average $\pi$. Changing the assigned endpoint value does not change the Fourier coefficients.
questions.rubric: Constant term: 3 points; sine and cosine coefficients: 3 points each; series: 3 points; endpoint values: 2 points.

questions.title: Scaling and differentiating delta
questions.question: Evaluate $\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\delta(2x-4)dx$ and $\int_{\mathbb R}(x^2+1)\delta\prime(x-1)dx$.
questions.hint: The scaling factor uses an absolute value. The action of $\delta\prime$ introduces a minus sign.
questions.solution:
We have $\delta(2x-4)=\frac12\delta(x-2)$, so the first result is $\frac12\cdot2^2=2$.

For the second, use $\langle\delta\prime(x-a),\varphi\rangle=-\varphi\prime(a)$ with $\varphi=x^2+1$ to obtain $-2$. This is the action of a compactly supported distribution on a smooth function; equivalently, insert a smooth cutoff equal to 1 near its support.
questions.rubric: Scaling factor: 3 points; first result: 3 points; derivative sign: 3 points; second result: 3 points.

questions.title: Carry the initial data into the transform
questions.question: Solve by Laplace transform: $y\prime\prime+2y\prime+y=1$, $y(0)=y\prime(0)=0$, $t\ge0$.
questions.hint: Transform the derivatives and insert the zero initial data. Solve for $Y(s)=1/[s(s+1)^2]$, then use partial fractions.
questions.solution:
The zero initial data give $\mathcal L[y\prime\prime]=s^2Y$ and $\mathcal L[y\prime]=sY$, hence $(s+1)^2Y=1/s$. Decompose

$$Y=\frac1s-\frac1{s+1}-\frac1{(s+1)^2}.$$

The inverse transform gives $y=1-e^{-t}-te^{-t}=1-(1+t)e^{-t}$. Differentiation gives $y\prime=te^{-t}$, so both initial conditions hold. Substitution into the differential equation gives the required right-hand side, 1.
questions.rubric: Transformed equation: 4 points; partial fractions: 3 points; inverse transform: 3 points; check: 2 points.

title: Differential equations and special functions
scope: Chapters 3–6 · Separation of variables, boundaries, series, spherical and Bessel functions, Green functions

questions.title: One vibration mode of a fixed string
questions.question: Solve $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$ with $0<x<L$, $u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0$, $u(x,0)=A\sin(\pi x/L)$, and $u_t(x,0)=0$.
questions.hint: The initial displacement already supplies a spatial mode. Only its time factor remains to be found.
questions.solution:
Set $u=T(t)\sin(\pi x/L)$. Substitution gives $T\prime\prime+\omega_1^2T=0$ and $\omega_1=c\pi/L$. The initial data give $T(0)=A,T\prime(0)=0$, so

$$u(x,t)=A\cos(c\pi t/L)\sin(\pi x/L).$$

The sine factor enforces the endpoints. The cosine is 1 at time zero, recovering the initial displacement, and its time derivative vanishes there.
questions.rubric: Spatial mode: 3 points; time equation: 3 points; constants: 4 points; verification: 2 points.

questions.title: A nonresonant forced string
questions.question: A fixed-end string satisfies $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}+F\sin(2\pi x/L)\cos\Omega t$ with zero initial displacement and velocity. Assume $\Omega\ge0$ and $\Omega\ne\omega_2=2\pi c/L$, and solve.
questions.hint: Set $u=q(t)\sin(2\pi x/L)$. Include a homogeneous term to cancel the particular solution at time zero.
questions.solution:
Substitution gives $q\prime\prime+\omega_2^2q=F\cos\Omega t$. A particular solution is $F\cos\Omega t/(\omega_2^2-\Omega^2)$. Add the homogeneous solution $B\cos\omega_2t+D\sin\omega_2t$; zero initial velocity gives $D=0$ and zero initial displacement gives $B=-F/(\omega_2^2-\Omega^2)$. Thus

$$u=\frac{F(\cos\Omega t-\cos\omega_2t)}{\omega_2^2-\Omega^2}\sin\frac{2\pi x}{L}.$$

At resonance, do not substitute $0/0$ directly into the quotient. Taking the limit gives $q=Ft\sin(\omega_2t)/(2\omega_2)$.
questions.rubric: Mode reduction: 3 points; particular and homogeneous solutions: 3 points; initial data: 3 points; result and resonance qualification: 3 points.

questions.title: A decaying series for heat
questions.question: Solve $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$ on $0<x<L$, with both endpoints zero, $u(x,0)=x(L-x)$, and $\kappa>0$.
questions.hint: Use a sine basis. Two integrations by parts give $n^{-3}$; then attach each mode’s decay factor.
questions.solution:
The zero endpoint conditions select $\sin(n\pi x/L)$, with time factor $e^{-\kappa(n\pi/L)^2t}$. Write $b_n=(2/L)\int_0^Lx(L-x)\sin(n\pi x/L)dx$. Let $a=n\pi/L$; two integrations by parts give integral $2[1-(-1)^n]/a^3$, hence

$$b_n=\frac{4L^2[1-(-1)^n]}{n^3\pi^3}.$$

Therefore

$$u(x,t)=\sum_{m=0}^\infty\frac{8L^2}{(2m+1)^3\pi^3}e^{-\kappa((2m+1)\pi/L)^2t}\sin\frac{(2m+1)\pi x}{L}.$$

Only odd modes remain, and higher frequencies decay faster. For $t>0$ the series is smooth; inside the interval, Fourier convergence recovers the initial data.
questions.rubric: Separation: 4 points; coefficients and parity: 5 points; solution: 3 points; physical interpretation: 2 points.

questions.title: A steady field in a rectangle
questions.question: In rectangle $0<x<a,0<y<b$, solve $u_{xx}+u_{yy}=0$ with boundary data $u(0,y)=u(a,y)=u(x,0)=0$ and $u(x,b)=V\sin(\pi x/a)$. Find $u$.
questions.hint: Use sine in the horizontal direction and hyperbolic sine vertically. Normalize using the top edge.
questions.solution:
Let $u=X(x)Y(y)$. Then $X\prime\prime+\lambda X=0$ and $Y\prime\prime-\lambda Y=0$. The zero left and right edges select $X=\sin(\pi x/a)$ and $\lambda=(\pi/a)^2$. The bottom edge gives $Y=B\sinh(\pi y/a)$; the top gives $B=V/\sinh(\pi b/a)$. Hence

$$u=V\frac{\sinh(\pi y/a)}{\sinh(\pi b/a)}\sin(\pi x/a).$$

The second derivatives in the two coordinates cancel, and all four boundary conditions hold.
questions.rubric: Separation signs and eigenvalue: 4 points; vertical solution: 4 points; boundary coefficient: 4 points; check: 2 points.

questions.title: Eigenvalues with mixed boundary conditions
questions.question: Find all eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, and squared norms for $-X\prime\prime=\lambda X$, $X\prime(0)=0,X(L)=0$.
questions.hint: For a positive eigenvalue start with cosine. Exclude zero and negative eigenvalues separately.
questions.solution:
For $\lambda=k^2>0$ the general solution is $A\cos kx+B\sin kx$. Condition $X\prime(0)=0$ gives $B=0$, and $X(L)=0$ gives $\cos kL=0$. Therefore

$$\lambda_n=((n+1/2)\pi/L)^2,\quad X_n=\cos((n+1/2)\pi x/L),\quad n=0,1,\ldots.$$

For $\lambda=0$, solution $X=A+Bx$ satisfies both boundaries only when it is zero. For $\lambda=-\mu^2$, use $X=A\cosh\mu x$; since $\cosh\mu L>0$, only the zero solution remains. The norm integral is $\int_0^L X_n^2dx=L/2$. Product-to-sum identities also verify orthogonality of different frequencies.
questions.rubric: Positive eigenvalues: 5 points; exclusion of zero and negative values: 4 points; norm: 3 points.

questions.title: Power series at an ordinary point
questions.question: Solve $y\prime\prime-xy=0$, $y(0)=1,y\prime(0)=0$ by power series through $x^9$.
questions.hint: Set $y=\sum a_nx^n$. Shift the index in $xy$ before comparing powers.
questions.solution:
We have $y\prime\prime=\sum_{n\ge0}(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n$ and $xy=\sum_{n\ge1}a_{n-1}x^n$. The constant coefficient gives $a_2=0$; coefficient $n\ge1$ gives $a_{n+2}=a_{n-1}/[(n+2)(n+1)]$. From $a_0=1,a_1=0$ we obtain $a_3=1/6,a_6=1/180,a_9=1/12960$; the other coefficients through degree 9 vanish.

$$y=1+\frac{x^3}{6}+\frac{x^6}{180}+\frac{x^9}{12960}+O(x^{12}).$$

The recurrence splits into chains spaced three indices apart. The initial data select one chain.
questions.rubric: Series substitution: 3 points; recurrence: 4 points; coefficients and result: 5 points.

questions.title: An axisymmetric steady field inside a sphere
questions.question: Inside sphere $r<a$, solve $\nabla^2u=0$, bounded at the center, with boundary value $u(a,\theta)=V\cos^2\theta$.
questions.hint: Use $\cos^2\theta=1/3+(2/3)P_2(\cos\theta)$. Discard radial terms that diverge at the center.
questions.solution:
The regular part of the axisymmetric expansion is $u=\sum_{l\ge0}A_lr^lP_l(\cos\theta)$. Since $P_0=1,P_2(\mu)=(3\mu^2-1)/2$, the boundary expansion is $V/3+(2V/3)P_2(\cos\theta)$. Only $l=0,2$ remain:

$$u=\frac V3+\frac{2V}{3}\left(\frac r a\right)^2P_2(\cos\theta).$$

Radial terms $r^{-l-1}$ diverge at the center and must be discarded. The value at the center is the spherical average of the boundary data, $V/3$.
questions.rubric: Boundary expansion: 4 points; discard singular terms: 3 points; solution: 3 points; check: 2 points.

questions.title: Images and a zero-boundary Green function
questions.question: In the upper half-space $z>0$, use convention $-\nabla^2G(\mathbf r,\mathbf r_0)=\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0)$, with $G=0$ on $z=0$ and $G\to0$ as $|\mathbf r|\to\infty$. Write the Green function and explain the role of each term.
questions.hint: Place the real source inside and its negative image outside.
questions.solution:
Let $\mathbf r_0=(x_0,y_0,z_0)$ and $z_0>0$, with reflected point $\mathbf r_0^*=(x_0,y_0,-z_0)$. The free-space fundamental solution is $1/(4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|)$, so

$$G=\frac1{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|}-\frac1{4\pi|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0^*|}.$$

Inside the domain, the second term has no singularity and is harmonic; the first supplies the unit source. On $z=0$ the two distances agree, so the terms cancel. Both terms decay at infinity. If the convention becomes $+\nabla^2G=\delta$, reverse the overall sign.
questions.rubric: Source and image positions: 3 points; Green function: 4 points; interior and boundary checks: 3 points; sign convention: 2 points.

title: Whole-book practice exam
scope: All six chapters · Choose a method, calculate, and check · 10 questions, 10 points each

questions.title: Recover a function from its real part
questions.question: An analytic function has real part $e^x\cos y$ and satisfies $f(0)=1+2i$. Find $f(z)$.
questions.hint: Recognize $e^z$, or integrate the Cauchy–Riemann equations.
questions.solution:
**Choose the method.** The real part is $u=e^x\cos y$ and the imaginary part $v$ is unknown. Use Cauchy–Riemann equations $v_y=u_x$, $v_x=-u_y$. First calculate $u_x=e^x\cos y$ and $u_y=-e^x\sin y$.

**Retain the integration function.** Integrate $v_y=e^x\cos y$ in $y$ to obtain $v=e^x\sin y+C(x)$. Since $x$ was held fixed, the integration constant may depend on $x$.

**Use the other equation.** $v_x=e^x\sin y+C^{\prime}(x)$ must equal $-u_y=e^x\sin y$. Hence $C^{\prime}=0$ and $C$ is a real constant.

**Use the value and check.** $f=u+iv=e^z+iC$; $f(0)=1+iC=1+2i$ fixes $C=2$, giving $f=e^z+2i$. Its real part is the stated $u$.
questions.rubric: Cauchy–Riemann integration: 4 points; constant: 3 points; analytic function: 3 points.

questions.title: Cancellation of zeros and a residue
questions.question: Classify the singularity of $f(z)=(e^z-1-z)/z^3$ at the origin and find its residue.
questions.hint: Expand the numerator through the cubic term. The denominator alone does not determine the pole order.
questions.solution:
**Expand the numerator first.** $e^z=1+z+z^2/2+z^3/6+z^4/24+\cdots$. Subtracting the constant and linear terms leaves degree two as the lowest nonzero power.

**Then divide.** $(e^z-1-z)/z^3=1/(2z)+1/6+z/24+\cdots$. The numerator cancels two powers from the cubic denominator.

**Read both answers.** The only negative power is $z^{-1}$, so the origin is a simple pole. Its residue is the coefficient $1/2$. Equivalently, $\lim_{z\to0}zf(z)=1/2\ne0$.
questions.rubric: Series: 4 points; pole order: 3 points; residue: 3 points.

questions.title: A shifted Fourier transform
questions.question: Let $a>0$ and $b\in\mathbb R$. Given $\mathcal F[e^{-a|x|}]=2a/(a^2+k^2)$, find the transform of $e^{-a|x-b|}$ using kernel $e^{-ikx}$.
questions.hint: Substitute $t=x-b$ and track the resulting phase factor.
questions.solution:
**Recognize translation.** Let $f(x)=e^{-a|x|}$; the target is $g(x)=f(x-b)$, translating the whole graph by $b$.

**Check the sign by substitution.** Set $t=x-b$, so $x=t+b$ and $e^{-ikx}=e^{-ikb}e^{-ikt}$. The translation factor is independent of $t$ and leaves the integral.

**Use the known transform.** $G(k)=e^{-ikb}2a/(a^2+k^2)$. Real $b$ and $k$ give $|e^{-ikb}|=1$, changing only phase. Setting $b=0$ recovers the original transform.
questions.rubric: Substitution: 3 points; phase sign: 3 points; result and interpretation: 4 points.

questions.title: Laplace delay and initial data
questions.question: Solve $y\prime+y=H(t-2)$, $y(0)=0$.
questions.hint: The right-hand side transforms to $e^{-2s}/s$. Use the time-delay rule when inverting.
questions.solution:
**Keep the delay in the transform.** Let $Y=\mathcal L[y]$. The derivative gives $sY-y(0)=sY$ and the step gives $e^{-2s}/s$, hence $(s+1)Y=e^{-2s}/s$.

**Find the undelayed response.** Decompose $1/[s(s+1)]=1/s-1/(s+1)$, whose original is $g(t)=1-e^{-t}$.

**Delay the entire function.** $e^{-2s}G(s)$ corresponds to $H(t-2)g(t-2)$, giving $y=H(t-2)[1-e^{-(t-2)}]$. Shift the time inside the brackets too.

**Check the pieces.** For $t<2$, $y=0$; for $t>2$, $y^{\prime}+y=1$. Since $g(0)=0$, the solution is continuous at switching and its first derivative has no extra delta term.
questions.rubric: Transformed equation: 4 points; partial fractions and delay: 4 points; continuity: 2 points.

questions.title: D’Alembert’s solution on an infinite string
questions.question: On an infinite string $u_{tt}=c^2u_{xx}$, with initial displacement $\phi(x)=e^{-x^2}$ and zero initial velocity, find and interpret the solution.
questions.hint: Split the initial displacement into two traveling waves, each with half the amplitude.
questions.solution:
**Let the domain select the method.** An infinite string with prescribed initial data suits d’Alembert’s formula. Denote initial displacement by $\phi$ and velocity by $\psi$.

**Insert zero initial velocity.** $u=[\phi(x-ct)+\phi(x+ct)]/2+(1/(2c))\int_{x-ct}^{x+ct}\psi(s)ds$. Here $\psi=0$, so the integral vanishes.

**Write and interpret the solution.** $u=\tfrac12[e^{-(x-ct)^2}+e^{-(x+ct)^2}]$. The first peak is at $x=ct$ and moves right; the second is at $x=-ct$ and moves left, each with half amplitude.

**Check initial data.** At $t=0$ the terms sum to $e^{-x^2}$. Their time derivatives carry chain-rule factors $-c$ and $c$ and cancel. Each traveling wave satisfies the wave equation.
questions.rubric: Formula: 4 points; substitution: 3 points; directions and initial conditions: 3 points.

questions.title: The constant heat mode
questions.question: A rod $0<x<L$ obeys $u_t=\kappa u_{xx}$ with $\kappa>0$, is insulated at both ends, and starts from $u(x,0)=T_0+A\cos(2\pi x/L)$. Find its temperature and long-time limit.
questions.hint: Use cosine modes. The constant mode has eigenvalue zero.
questions.solution:
**Read the boundary first.** Insulation means $u_x(0,t)=u_x(L,t)=0$, selecting cosines. A constant is also a valid mode; retain the average temperature $T_0$.

**Only two modes are needed.** The initial profile is already $T_0+A\cos(2\pi x/L)$, so set $u=T_0+q(t)\cos(2\pi x/L)$. Two spatial derivatives give factor $-(2\pi/L)^2$.

**Solve the time coefficient.** The heat equation gives $q^{\prime}=-4\kappa\pi^2q/L^2$ with $q(0)=A$, so $u=T_0+A e^{-4\kappa\pi^2t/L^2}\cos(2\pi x/L)$.

**Check long-time behavior.** Since $\kappa>0$, the nonconstant term decays and $u\to T_0$. The cosine has zero average, so the rod’s mean temperature remains $T_0$ throughout.
questions.rubric: Basis and zero mode: 3 points; solution: 4 points; limit and meaning: 3 points.

questions.title: Abel’s formula and its conditions
questions.question: For $y\prime\prime+2y\prime+y=0$ and the given solutions $y_1=e^{-x},y_2=xe^{-x}$, calculate $W=y_1y_2\prime-y_1\prime y_2$ and check Abel’s formula.
questions.hint: The coefficient of $y\prime$ is 2, so $W=C e^{-2x}$.
questions.solution:
**Differentiate first.** $y_1^{\prime}=-e^{-x}$. The product rule gives $y_2^{\prime}=e^{-x}-xe^{-x}=(1-x)e^{-x}$.

**Use the stated determinant order.** $W=y_1y_2^{\prime}-y_1^{\prime}y_2=(1-x)e^{-2x}+xe^{-2x}=e^{-2x}$. Subtracting the negative second term gives a plus.

**Check independently with Abel’s formula.** The first-derivative coefficient is two, so $W^{\prime}=-2W$ and $W=C e^{-2x}$. Directly, $W(0)=1$, hence $C=1$, consistent with the determinant.

**Interpret the result.** For every finite real $x$, $W\ne0$. The two solutions are independent and form a fundamental solution pair for the second-order equation.
questions.rubric: Derivatives and Wronskian: 4 points; Abel check: 4 points; independence: 2 points.

questions.title: Orthogonal expansion in Legendre polynomials
questions.question: Expand $x^2$ on $[-1,1]$ in Legendre polynomials and evaluate $\int_{-1}^1x^2P_2(x)dx$.
questions.hint: Use $P_2=(3x^2-1)/2$ and the norm $2/(2l+1)$.
questions.solution:
**Express the power in the requested basis.** Use $P_0(x)=1$ and $P_2(x)=(3x^2-1)/2$. Solve for $x^2$ to obtain $x^2=P_0/3+2P_2/3$.

**Multiply by the target polynomial and integrate.** $\int x^2P_2=\tfrac13\int P_0P_2+\tfrac23\int P_2^2$, all over $[-1,1]$. Orthogonality makes the first term zero.

**Insert the squared norm.** $\int_{-1}^1P_2^2dx=2/(2\cdot2+1)=2/5$, giving $(2/3)(2/5)=4/15$. The expansion coefficient $2/3$ is not itself the integral.

**Check directly.** Integrating $x^2P_2=(3x^4-x^2)/2$ gives $[3(2/5)-2/3]/2=4/15$, agreeing with projection.
questions.rubric: Expansion: 4 points; orthogonality and norm: 3 points; result: 3 points.

questions.title: The lowest radial mode of a circular membrane
questions.question: A circular membrane of radius $a$ obeys $u_{tt}=c^2\nabla^2u$, has a fixed edge, and is axisymmetric and bounded at the center. Find its radial eigenfunctions and natural angular frequencies. For initial shape $A J_0(j_{0,1}r/a)$ and zero initial velocity, find its motion.
questions.hint: Discard $Y_0$ at the center. The edge requires $J_0(ka)=0$.
questions.solution:
**Use symmetry to remove the angular variable.** The radial equation is $R^{\prime\prime}+R^{\prime}/r+k^2R=0$, with solutions $J_0(kr)$ and $Y_0(kr)$. Boundedness at the center removes $Y_0$.

**Let the boundary select frequencies.** The fixed rim requires $J_0(ka)=0$. With $j_{0,n}$ the $n$th positive zero of $J_0$, $k_n=j_{0,n}/a$ and $R_n=J_0(j_{0,n}r/a)$.

**Pair space with time.** The time equation is $q_n^{\prime\prime}+c^2k_n^2q_n=0$, giving natural angular frequency $\omega_n=ck_n=cj_{0,n}/a$. Ordinary frequency is this divided by $2\pi$.

**Use the single-mode data.** Only the first radial mode is present initially. Zero initial velocity removes the time sine, giving $u=A J_0(j_{0,1}r/a)\cos(cj_{0,1}t/a)$. Check the rim at $r=a$ and initial shape at $t=0$.
questions.rubric: Radial equation: 3 points; zeros and frequencies: 4 points; single-mode solution: 3 points.

questions.title: A point source and the Green-function sign
questions.question: Solve $-\nabla^2u=q\delta(\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0)$ with decay at infinity. Check normalization using the flux through a small sphere.
questions.hint: Use $\nabla^2(1/r)=-4\pi\delta$. The outward radial derivative is negative.
questions.solution:
**Fix the sign first.** Since $\nabla^2(1/R)=-4\pi\delta$ and the operator is the negative Laplacian, try $u=C/R$ with $R=|\mathbf r-\mathbf r_0|$.

**Determine the constant by flux.** Integrate over a radius-$\varepsilon$ ball centered at the source. The divergence theorem gives $-\int_{S_\varepsilon}\partial_nu\,dS=q$.

**Insert the radial derivative and area.** The outward derivative is $\partial_nu=-C/\varepsilon^2$ and the area is $4\pi\varepsilon^2$. Hence $4\pi C=q$ and $u=q/(4\pi R)$; the two minus signs cancel.

**Check the regions.** Outside the source, $1/R$ is harmonic and decays at infinity. Verify the delta at the source through integration or distributions, not ordinary pointwise second derivatives.
